descripcion_es: Describing the weather, the seasons and the climate of a place.
resumen: Vocabulary for saying what the weather is like, talking about forecasts and seasons, and comparing the climate of different places.

explicacion.texto: We describe the weather with It's + adjective (It's sunny, It's cold) or with verbs (It's raining, It snowed last night). We don't say “It makes cold”: Spanish “hace” is not translated as make.

filas: a question about the weather (es: ¿Qué tiempo hace?)
What's the weather like in Dublin?
with sun / with clouds (es: soleado / nublado)
with rain / with wind (es: lluvioso / con viento)
with fog / with storms (es: con niebla / tormentoso)
It was foggy on the motorway.
very high temperature / pleasantly high (es: caluroso / templado, agradable)
a bit cold / cold / very cold (es: fresco / frío / helador)
rain / snow is falling now (es: está lloviendo / nevando)
a short period of rain (es: chubasco)
a lot of rain (es: lluvia intensa)
a storm with thunder and lightning (es: tormenta eléctrica)
There was a thunderstorm last night.
the four seasons (es: primavera / verano / otoño / invierno)
The colours in the fall are amazing.
what the weather will be like (es: previsión del tiempo)
The forecast says it will rain.
the usual weather of a place (es: clima)
not too hot or cold / without rain / with wet air (es: suave / seco / húmedo)
The summers are hot and humid.
a period of very hot weather (es: ola de calor)
a long time without rain (es: sequía)
to become wet / completely wet (es: mojarse / calarse)
I got soaked on the way home.

items: Weather is uncountable: What terrible weather!, not “a terrible weather”.
Weather is the conditions at a particular time; climate is the usual weather of an area.
Seasons take in: in summer / in the summer.

ejemplos.frase: It's been raining all day, so we stayed at home.
ejemplos.traduccion: Lleva lloviendo todo el día, así que nos quedamos en casa.

ejemplos.frase: The forecast says it will be sunny tomorrow.
ejemplos.traduccion: La previsión dice que mañana hará sol.

ejemplos.frase: In winter it's freezing in Burgos.
ejemplos.traduccion: En invierno hace un frío helador en Burgos.

ejemplos.frase: The Canary Islands have a mild climate all year round.
ejemplos.traduccion: Canarias tiene un clima suave todo el año.

ejemplos.frase: We got soaked because we didn't have an umbrella.
ejemplos.traduccion: Nos calamos porque no llevábamos paraguas.

ejemplos.frase: What lovely weather! Let's have lunch outside.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: It makes a lot of heat.
Today the climate is very cloudy.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: Today the weather is very cloudy.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: The weather on a particular day is weather.

ejercicios.frase: What's the weather ___ in London today?
ejercicios.explicacion: It is the fixed formula from the table of expressions for asking about the weather: What's the weather like? The clue is the subject the weather, followed by a place and a time (in London today). Here like is a preposition, and the literal question would be “how is the weather?”. You can't replace it with how: in English you say How's the weather? or What's the weather like?, but you can't mix them.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Spanish “¿Qué tiempo hace?” is What's the weather like?

errores_previstos.respuesta: how
errores_previstos.explicacion: “What's the weather how” doesn't exist: how only works in the other formula, How's the weather?, without what or like.

errores_previstos.respuesta: as
errores_previstos.explicacion: As is used in comparisons or for roles, but in this fixed question only like is possible.

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with the correct form of the verb rain.
ejercicios.explicacion: The unit explains that we can describe the weather with verbs, and that for what is happening now we use the present continuous: It's raining. The clue is It's before the gap and the situation at this moment (taking an umbrella). That's why you need the -ing form of rain: raining. The subject is impersonal it, as in It's snowing.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Rain is falling now: it's raining.
ejercicios.traduccion: Coge el paraguas. Está lloviendo fuera.

errores_previstos.respuesta: rain
errores_previstos.explicacion: After It's (it is) you need the -ing form for something happening now; “It's rain” is not correct.

errores_previstos.respuesta: rainy
errores_previstos.explicacion: It's rainy exists and describes a rainy day or area in general, but the instruction asks for the form of the verb rain to say that it is raining now.

errores_previstos.respuesta: rainning
errores_previstos.explicacion: Spelling mistake: rain doesn't double the n, because it ends in two vowels plus a consonant; it is spelt raining.

ejercicios.explicacion: It is a word from the second table: heatwave, a period of several days with exceptionally high temperatures. The clue is the figure of 44 degrees and the article the, which needs a noun. It is written as one word (heatwave) or two (heat wave); both spellings are correct, so both are accepted.
ejercicios.traduccion: Durante la ola de calor las temperaturas llegaron a 44 grados.

errores_previstos.respuesta: wave of heat
errores_previstos.explicacion: It is a calque of Spanish “ola de calor”; in English the describing noun comes first: heatwave.

errores_previstos.respuesta: hot wave
errores_previstos.explicacion: It is not the fixed expression; the term is heatwave, with the noun heat, not the adjective hot.

ejercicios.explicacion: The unit gives it in the final list: seasons take in (in winter or in the winter). The clue is the name of the season, winter, after the gap. It is the same preposition as with months and years (in August, in 2020). Spanish “en invierno” is the same, but don't use on, which is for specific days.
ejercicios.traduccion: Aquí nieva a menudo en invierno.

errores_previstos.respuesta: on
errores_previstos.explicacion: On is used with days and dates (on Monday, on 5 May), not with seasons.

errores_previstos.respuesta: at
errores_previstos.explicacion: At is used with times and specific moments (at night, at Christmas), not with seasons.

ejercicios.frase: It's very ___ today; my hat flew away!
ejercicios.explicacion: The rule It's + adjective for describing the weather applies, with the adjective windy (with a lot of wind) from the first table. The clue is in the second part of the sentence: the hat flies away, and only the wind can do that. Windy is formed with wind + y, like sunny, cloudy or foggy.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: If your hat flies away, it's windy.
ejercicios.traduccion: Hace mucho viento hoy; ¡mi sombrero ha salido volando!

por_opcion.windy: Correct: windy means there is a lot of wind, and that is what makes the hat fly away.
por_opcion.foggy: It means there is fog; it makes it hard to see, but it doesn't blow hats away.
por_opcion.sunny: It means the sun is shining; it doesn't explain why the hat flies away.

ejercicios.frase: I can't see the road. It's really ___.
ejercicios.explicacion: Again It's + adjective, now with foggy, which the first table explains as “with fog”. The clue is “I can't see the road”: what stops you seeing is the fog. Note that Spanish says “hay niebla”, with haber, while English uses it + be + adjective: It's foggy.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: If you can't see, it's foggy.
ejercicios.traduccion: No veo la carretera. Hay mucha niebla.

por_opcion.foggy: Correct: foggy, with fog, explains why you can't see the road.
por_opcion.warm: It means pleasantly hot; the temperature doesn't stop you seeing the road.
por_opcion.dry: It means without rain; it doesn't make it harder to see either.

ejercicios.frase: Southern Spain has a hot, dry ___.
ejercicios.explicacion: The distinction in the unit between weather, the conditions at a particular time, and climate, the usual weather of an area, applies. The clue is that the sentence is about a whole region (Southern Spain) and a permanent feature, with the present simple has. That's why only climate is possible; also, a hot, dry climate takes an article because climate is countable.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: The usual weather of an area is climate.
ejercicios.traduccion: El sur de España tiene un clima cálido y seco.

por_opcion.climate: Correct: climate is the usual weather of a place, which is what is described here.
por_opcion.weather: Weather is the conditions on a particular day or period, and it is also uncountable, so it can't go with a.
por_opcion.time: Time is chronological time (hours, minutes), never the weather: it is a false friend of Spanish “tiempo”.

ejercicios.frase: There hasn't been any rain for months. The ___ is a disaster for farmers.
ejercicios.explicacion: It is vocabulary from the second table: drought, a long time without rain (es: sequía). The clue is the first sentence, “it hasn't rained for months”, which describes exactly a drought. Be careful with the pronunciation: drought rhymes with out, although it is spelt with ough.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: A long time without rain is a drought.
ejercicios.traduccion: No ha llovido en meses. La sequía es un desastre para los agricultores.

por_opcion.drought: Correct: a drought is the result of months without rain.
por_opcion.flood: It means a large amount of water covering land, the exact opposite: too much water.
por_opcion.shower: It means a short period of rain; it doesn't fit with months without rain.

ejercicios.frase: In August it makes a lot of heat in Córdoba.
respuestas: In August it's very hot in Córdoba.
In August it is very hot in Córdoba.
ejercicios.explicacion: It is the typical mistake the unit mentions first: Spanish “hacer calor” is not translated with make, but with It's + adjective. The clue is the calqued structure “it makes a lot of heat”. The correct form is It's very hot or It is very hot: the adjective hot and the intensifier very replace “mucho calor”. Both versions, with or without the contraction, are correct.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Spanish “hace calor” is it's hot, not make heat.
ejercicios.traduccion: En agosto hace mucho calor en Córdoba.

errores_previstos.respuesta: In August it makes a lot of heat in Córdoba.
errores_previstos.explicacion: That leaves the sentence uncorrected: make is not used to talk about the weather; use It's + adjective.

errores_previstos.respuesta: In August it does a lot of heat in Córdoba.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Changing make to do doesn't help: English doesn't use any verb meaning “hacer” for the weather.

errores_previstos.respuesta: In August it is very heat in Córdoba.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Heat is a noun; after it is you need the adjective hot.

ejercicios.frase: We had a terrible weather on holiday.
respuestas: We had terrible weather on holiday.
ejercicios.explicacion: The rule from the list in the unit applies: weather is uncountable, so it takes no a and no plural. The clue is the article a before the adjective terrible, a calque of Spanish “un tiempo horrible”. The correct sentence drops the article: We had terrible weather. The same happens in exclamations: What terrible weather!
ejercicios.traduccion: Tuvimos un tiempo horrible en las vacaciones.

errores_previstos.respuesta: We had a terrible weather on holiday.
errores_previstos.explicacion: That leaves the sentence uncorrected: weather is uncountable and doesn't take a.

errores_previstos.respuesta: We had terrible weathers on holiday.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Weather has no plural in this sense; just remove the article.

ejercicios.frase: What's the climate like today? Is it raining?
respuestas: What's the weather like today? Is it raining?
What is the weather like today? Is it raining?
ejercicios.explicacion: It is the weather versus climate distinction from the unit. The clue is today and the question about whether it is raining at the moment: it is about the weather on a particular day, not the usual conditions of an area. So you need to change climate to weather, and the formula is What's the weather like today?
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Today's conditions are weather, not climate.

errores_previstos.respuesta: What's the climate like today? Is it raining?
errores_previstos.explicacion: That leaves the sentence uncorrected: climate is the usual weather of a place, not today's weather.

errores_previstos.respuesta: What's the time like today? Is it raining?
errores_previstos.explicacion: Time is chronological time; for the conditions outside we say weather.

respuestas: The forecast says it will rain
ejercicios.explicacion: Use the expression (weather) forecast from the second table, which appears in an almost identical example in the unit. The order is subject (The forecast) + verb (says) + that-clause (it will rain), with the impersonal weather it and the future will. In English the conjunction that can be left out, so it doesn't appear.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: The forecast says it will rain.

errores_previstos.respuesta: The forecast says will rain it
errores_previstos.explicacion: The subject it goes before the verb; in English you can't leave it out or move it after the verb as in Spanish.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Says the forecast it will rain
errores_previstos.explicacion: In a statement the subject (the forecast) goes before the verb says.

respuestas: It was five degrees below zero
ejercicios.explicacion: It is the expression below zero from the first table, combined with It + be for temperature. The order is It was + number + degrees + below zero, as in Spanish: “cinco grados bajo cero”. The past was shows that it describes a past situation.

errores_previstos.respuesta: It was below zero five degrees
errores_previstos.explicacion: The number and degrees go before below zero, as in Spanish: five degrees below zero.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Was it five degrees below zero
errores_previstos.explicacion: That is question order; the sentence required is a statement.

ejercicios.frase: In New England the leaves turn red in the ___.
ejercicios.explicacion: The unit says that in American English autumn is fall, compared with British autumn. There are two clues: the instruction asks for the American term, and New England is a region of the United States. Fall comes from “the fall of the leaves”. It takes the, in the fall, like the season in the unit.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: In American English autumn is fall.
ejercicios.traduccion: En Nueva Inglaterra las hojas se vuelven rojas en otoño.

errores_previstos.respuesta: autumn
errores_previstos.explicacion: Autumn is correct in meaning, but it is the British word; the instruction asks for the American one.

errores_previstos.respuesta: fell
errores_previstos.explicacion: Fell is the past of the verb fall; the season is fall.

ejercicios.frase: We walked home in the storm and got completely ___.
ejercicios.explicacion: It is the expression get wet / get soaked from the second table: get soaked means to become completely wet (es: calarse). The clue is completely and the situation of walking in a storm. Get + past participle expresses a change of state (to become), so soaked is a past participle. It is stronger than get wet.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: To get wet through is get soaked.
ejercicios.traduccion: Volvimos a casa andando bajo la tormenta y nos calamos por completo.

por_opcion.soaked: Correct: get soaked means to become completely wet, which is what happens when you walk in a storm.
por_opcion.humid: Humid describes wet air in a climate, not a person wet from the rain.
por_opcion.dried: Get dried would mean to become dry, the exact opposite of what happens in a storm.

descripcion_larga_es: Vocabulary for describing the weather, the seasons, forecasts and the climate of a place. It is one of the most common topics of conversation in English, especially in the United Kingdom, and it comes up in almost every basic-level oral exam. Spanish speakers find it difficult because they calque “hace frío” with make and confuse weather (es: tiempo) with climate (es: clima).

contexto.que_es: It is the basic vocabulary for saying what the weather is like: adjectives such as sunny, cloudy or windy, verbs such as rain and snow, phenomena such as heatwave or drought, and the difference between weather, the conditions at a particular time, and climate, the usual weather of an area. It also includes the seasons and how to express temperatures.
contexto.por_que_importa: Talking about the weather is the most common way to start a conversation in English, and in the United Kingdom it is almost a social ritual. Using make for heat or cold, or saying climate when talking about today, immediately shows a calque from Spanish. In an A2 oral exam it is a typical topic for description and short conversation.
contexto.cuando_se_usa: We use it when greeting people or chatting, commenting on a forecast, planning a trip or comparing countries. The clearest signal is the question What's the weather like? or a reference to today, tomorrow or next week. Where Spanish says “hace calor” or “hay sol”, English uses It's + adjective: It's hot, It's sunny.
